newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. envoy tries to halt Iraqi Kurdish fighting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy tries to halt Iraqi Kurdish fighting.

text.p: A U.S. envoy has embarked on a mission to try to halt fighting between rival Kurdish factions in northern Iraq, a region protected by a U.S.-led alliance from the forces of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

Robert Pelletreau, U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, will meet Massoud Barzani, leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), in southeast Turkey on Monday, a Turkish Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.
Pelletreau will also hold talks with Barzani's long-time adversary, Jalal Talabani, who heads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), in Ankara later in the week, the official said.

The KDP, which received backing from Saddam's forces during earlier fighting in August, has launched an offensive aimed at the PUK stronghold of Sulaimaniya, the region's biggest city with a population of around one million people, to snive was attempting to take the dam in a push to recapture their rival's stronghold Sulaimaniya.
Forces loyal to the two Kurdish warlords were engaged in a bitter fight on Sunday for control of the strategic Dukan Dam.
Witnesses said Talabani's forces had stalled a KDP advance about five km (three miles) from the dam.

Barzani's militia could not move a 155-mm artillery gun, which they had used earlier in the day, closer to the dam because of rugged terrain, KDP fighters said. The defending forces fired lighter artillery rounds.
Dukan lies on a main road to the city from territory held by Barzani to the west and north.
Control of would give either leader a strong card to play at the negotating table.
The United States has called on both sides to end the fighting, which has criss-crossed the Western-protected mountainous region since August.
Barzani tilted the balance in his favour in late August when he joined with armour-backed Iraqi troops to take the city of Arbil from Talabani.
The return of Baghdad to the region after a five-year absence in the wake of the 1991 Gulf War ended U.S. military, aid and intelligence programmes there.
Around 700 Iraqi Kurds linked to U.S.-affiliated organisations took refuge in Turkey at the weekend because of the latest fighting.
More than 2,000 other Iraqi Kurds with links to Washington fled the region in fear of Saddam last month.
Barzani told Pelletreau in a meeting in Turkey last month that his alliance with President Saddam Hussein was a one-off deal to counter what he says is Iranian backing for the PUK.
But Barzani threatened last week to call on Saddam's help again if things were not going the KDP's way on the battlefield.

Washington tried twice in vain last year to get the two Kurdish groups to bury their differences, many of which go back decades. Two rounds of U.S.-brokered peace talks in Ireland failed to come up with a lasting solution.
